1.summary: The eternal Word who was with God and was God becomes flesh; John the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God, and the first disciples begin to follow him.
1.lookfor: Notice how the opening echoes the first words of Genesis, and how each new disciple brings someone else to Jesus.

names.name: Levites
names.gloss: Members of the priestly tribe who served in the temple, sent to question John.

names.name: Bethany
names.gloss: A place across the Jordan where John baptized, not the village near Jerusalem.

names.name: Andrew
names.gloss: Simon Peter's brother, first a disciple of John.

names.name: Cephas
names.gloss: Aramaic for rock, the name Jesus gives Simon; Peter is the Greek form.

names.name: Philip
names.gloss: A disciple from Bethsaida.

names.name: Nathanael
names.gloss: A disciple from Cana, possibly the Bartholomew of the other Gospels.

insights.title: In the beginning
insights.body: "In the beginning was the Word" (1:1) deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. John retells creation with Jesus present at the start: through him all things were made (1:3).

insights.title: Logos
insights.body: John calls Jesus the Logos, the Word (1:1). Greek thinkers used logos for the reason ordering the universe; Jewish writers spoke of God's word and wisdom creating the world. John meets both audiences and then says something neither expected: the Word became flesh (1:14).

insights.title: He pitched his tent
insights.body: "The Word became flesh, and lived among us" (1:14). The Greek verb means to pitch a tent, recalling the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt with Israel in the wilderness.

insights.title: The Lamb of God
insights.body: John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (1:29). The image gathers the Passover lamb, the daily temple lambs and Isaiah's servant led like a lamb to slaughter.

insights.title: The tenth hour
insights.body: Two disciples follow Jesus and stay with him; it was about the tenth hour (1:39), about four in the afternoon. The time is the kind of remembered detail an eyewitness keeps.

insights.title: Jacob's ladder
insights.body: Jesus tells Nathanael he will see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man (1:51). In Jacob's dream the angels used a ladder; now Jesus himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth.

insights.title: Come and see
insights.body: Philip doesn't argue with Nathanael's doubt; he says, "Come and see" (1:46). Who might you invite simply to come and see?

2.summary: At a wedding in Cana Jesus turns water into wine, his first sign, and in Jerusalem he drives the traders from the temple and speaks of raising the temple of his body.
2.lookfor: Notice what the water jars were for, and how the disciples understand Jesus' words about the temple only later.

names.name: Cana
names.gloss: A village in Galilee a few kilometers from Nazareth.

names.name: Capernaum
names.gloss: A fishing town on the Sea of Galilee.

insights.title: Running out of wine
insights.body: Weddings lasted up to a week, and running out of wine would shame the family before the village. Mary notices and tells Jesus (2:3).

insights.title: Woman
insights.body: Jesus addresses his mother as "Woman" (2:4), which sounds cold in English but was a respectful form of address. He uses it again from the cross as he entrusts her to the beloved disciple.

insights.title: Six stone jars
insights.body: The water came from six stone jars used for Jewish purification, each holding two or three metretes, perhaps 80 to 120 liters (2:6). Jesus fills the vessels of the old rites with abundant new wine.

insights.title: The first of the signs
insights.body: John calls the miracle the first of his signs, revealing his glory (2:11). John records seven signs before the cross, each pointing beyond itself to who Jesus is.

insights.title: Forty-six years
insights.body: The leaders say the temple has been under construction for forty-six years (2:20). Herod began rebuilding about 20 BC, which places this scene around AD 27 or 28.

insights.title: Early or late?
insights.body: Matthew, Mark and Luke place the temple clearing in Jesus' last week; John places it at the start. Some think there were two clearings; others think John placed it first for theological reasons. Either way, Jesus presents himself as the true temple.

insights.title: Do whatever he tells you
insights.body: Mary tells the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it" (2:5). What has Jesus told you that you haven't yet done?

3.summary: Jesus tells the Pharisee Nicodemus that he must be born from above, speaks of God's love for the world, and John the Baptist says Jesus must increase while he decreases.
3.lookfor: Notice when Nicodemus comes, how he misunderstands, and the contrast between light and darkness.

names.name: Nicodemus
names.gloss: A Pharisee and member of the ruling council who comes to Jesus at night.

names.name: Enon
names.gloss: A place with plentiful water where John baptized; its location is uncertain.

names.name: Salim
names.gloss: A town near Enon; its exact site is unknown.

insights.title: Born anew, born from above
insights.body: The Greek word anōthen means both again and from above (3:3). Nicodemus hears again and asks about re-entering the womb; Jesus means a birth from God. Translations differ, and John likely intends both senses.

insights.title: Water and Spirit
insights.body: Jesus speaks of being born of water and Spirit (3:5). A teacher of Israel should have known Ezekiel's promise: clean water sprinkled, a new heart and God's Spirit within.

insights.title: The lifted serpent
insights.body: As Moses lifted up the bronze serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up (3:14). In John, "lifted up" means both the cross and exaltation. Those who looked at the serpent lived.

insights.title: God so loved the world
insights.body: John 3:16 is perhaps the best-known verse in the Bible. The world here (kosmos) is often the rebellious world in John, which makes the love more startling: God gives his only Son to the world that rejects him.

insights.title: Night and light
insights.body: Nicodemus comes at night (3:2), and the chapter speaks of people loving darkness rather than light (3:19). He returns later, defending Jesus and finally helping bury him, moving into the light.

insights.title: The bridegroom's friend
insights.body: John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom (3:29), who arranged the wedding and rejoiced to hear the groom's voice. His joy is to step aside: he must increase, but I must decrease (3:30).

insights.title: Coming at night
insights.body: Nicodemus was curious but careful, coming when no one would see. What questions about Jesus do you keep in the dark?

4.summary: At Jacob's well Jesus offers living water to a Samaritan woman, reveals himself as the Messiah, and many Samaritans believe; then he heals an official's son from a distance.
4.lookfor: Watch how the conversation moves from water to worship to the Messiah, and who the woman tells.

names.name: Sychar
names.gloss: A Samaritan town near Jacob's well, by Mount Gerizim.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: Israel's ancestor, who gave this land and well to his son Joseph.

names.name: Samaritans
names.gloss: People of Samaria who worshiped at Mount Gerizim and kept only the five books of Moses.

insights.title: Noon at the well
insights.body: The woman comes about the sixth hour, around noon (4:6), the hottest time, perhaps to avoid other women. A Jewish man speaking with a Samaritan woman and asking to drink from her jar broke several social rules at once (4:9).

insights.title: Living water
insights.body: Living water meant running water from a spring, better than a cistern (4:10). Jesus means a spring welling up to eternal life. Jeremiah called God the spring of living water his people had abandoned.

insights.title: This mountain
insights.body: The woman raises the old dispute: Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim, Jews in Jerusalem (4:20). Jesus says the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship in spirit and truth, in neither place only.

insights.title: I am he
insights.body: When the woman mentions the Messiah, Jesus says, "I am he" (4:26); the Greek is simply egō eimi, "I am." It is the first of many "I am" sayings in John that echo God's name revealed to Moses.

insights.title: She left her jar
insights.body: The woman leaves her water jar and goes back to tell the town (4:28). Many Samaritans believe because of her word, then because they hear Jesus themselves (4:39-42).

insights.title: Savior of the world
insights.body: The Samaritans call Jesus "the Savior of the world" (4:42). Outsiders, not his own people, give him this title, anticipating the mission to Samaria in Acts.

insights.title: Thirsty again
insights.body: Everyone who drinks this water will thirst again (4:13). What do you keep returning to that never quite satisfies?

5.summary: Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath, then defends his work as the Son doing what the Father does.
5.lookfor: Notice why the leaders want to kill Jesus (5:18), and the list of witnesses he calls.

names.name: Bethesda
names.gloss: A pool in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate, surrounded by covered porches.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: Israel's lawgiver, whose writings Jesus says testify about him.

insights.title: Five porches
insights.body: John describes a pool with five covered porches (5:2). Excavations near St Anne's Church in Jerusalem uncovered twin pools with colonnades, matching his description.

insights.title: The missing verse
insights.body: Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is absent from the earliest manuscripts, so many Bibles omit or bracket it. Verse 7 shows the popular belief that the first one in after the stirring was healed.

insights.title: Do you want to be made well?
insights.body: Jesus asks a man ill for thirty-eight years if he wants to be well (5:6). The man answers with an excuse about having no one to help. Jesus heals him anyway with a word.

insights.title: Equal with God
insights.body: Jesus defends healing on the Sabbath: my Father is still working, so I am working (5:17). The leaders understand him to be calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God (5:18).

insights.title: Life and judgment
insights.body: The Father has given the Son authority to give life and to judge (5:21-27). Those who hear and believe already have eternal life and have passed from death to life (5:24).

insights.title: Moses wrote about me
insights.body: Jesus lists his witnesses: John, his works, the Father, the Scriptures, and finally Moses, who wrote about him (5:46). The leaders searched the Scriptures but missed the one they point to.

insights.title: Searching the Scriptures
insights.body: You search the Scriptures, Jesus says, yet you won't come to me (5:39-40). How can Bible reading become a way to meet Jesus rather than avoid him?

6.summary: Jesus feeds five thousand, walks on the sea, and declares himself the bread of life; many disciples leave over his hard words, but Peter says they have nowhere else to go.
6.lookfor: Watch how the crowd wants more bread, while Jesus offers himself as the bread from heaven.

names.name: Tiberias
names.gloss: A city on the Sea of Galilee built by Herod Antipas; the lake was also named after it.

names.name: Simon
names.gloss: Simon Peter; also the father of Judas Iscariot is named Simon.

names.name: Judas
names.gloss: Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, who would betray Jesus.

insights.title: Barley loaves
insights.body: Only John says the boy's five loaves were barley (6:9), the bread of the poor. Elisha fed a hundred with twenty barley loaves; Jesus feeds thousands with five.

insights.title: Passover was near
insights.body: John notes that Passover was near (6:4). The feeding, the sea crossing and the talk of manna all echo the exodus.

insights.title: It is I
insights.body: Walking on the sea, Jesus says, "It is I. Don't be afraid" (6:20); the Greek is again egō eimi, "I am." In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves.

insights.title: The true bread from heaven
insights.body: The crowd recalls the manna Moses gave; Jesus says the true bread from heaven is the one who comes down and gives life to the world (6:32-33). Then he says, "I am the bread of life" (6:35), the first of seven "I am" sayings with an image.

insights.title: Eat my flesh
insights.body: Jesus says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life (6:54). Catholic, Orthodox and many other traditions read this in the light of the Lord's Supper; others stress that it means believing in him. All agree it points to his self-giving death.

insights.title: Many turned back
insights.body: Many disciples find the teaching too hard and leave (6:66). Jesus doesn't soften it; he asks the twelve whether they want to go too.

insights.title: To whom would we go?
insights.body: Peter answers, "Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life" (6:68). When following Jesus is hard, what keeps you from leaving?

7.summary: At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus teaches in the temple amid argument about who he is, offers rivers of living water to the thirsty, and the leaders' attempt to arrest him fails.
7.lookfor: Notice the crowd's arguments about where the Messiah comes from, and what Jesus cries out on the last day of the feast.

names.name: Nicodemus
names.gloss: The Pharisee who visited Jesus at night, now defending fair hearing.

names.name: Bethlehem
names.gloss: David's town, where the Messiah was expected to come from.

insights.title: The Feast of Tabernacles
insights.body: Tabernacles, or Booths, was an autumn harvest festival when people lived in shelters to remember the wilderness (7:2). It was one of the three pilgrim feasts, and Jerusalem filled with crowds.

insights.title: His brothers didn't believe
insights.body: Jesus' brothers urge him to show himself publicly, for even they did not believe in him (7:5). After the resurrection his brother James became a leader of the Jerusalem church.

insights.title: Water poured out
insights.body: Each morning of the feast, priests carried water from the pool of Siloam and poured it at the altar, praying for rain. On the last great day Jesus stands and cries: if anyone is thirsty, come to me and drink (7:37).

insights.title: Rivers of living water
insights.body: Jesus promises rivers of living water flowing from within, and John explains he meant the Spirit (7:38-39). Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple bringing life wherever it went.

insights.title: No one ever spoke like this
insights.body: The officers sent to arrest Jesus come back empty-handed: no man ever spoke like this man (7:46). Nicodemus asks that Jesus get a fair hearing and is mocked (7:50-52).

insights.title: A story in brackets
insights.body: The story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) is missing from the earliest manuscripts and appears in different places in others. Many scholars consider it a genuine early tradition about Jesus added later; many Bibles bracket it.

insights.title: If anyone is thirsty
insights.body: Jesus' invitation is simple: come and drink. What are you thirsty for that only he can give?

8.summary: Jesus forgives a woman caught in adultery, declares himself the light of the world, and in a sharp debate about Abraham claims, "Before Abraham came into existence, I AM."
8.lookfor: Watch how the argument about who are Abraham's true children builds to Jesus' final claim and the crowd picking up stones.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: Father of the Jewish people, to whom God gave the covenant promises.

insights.title: Writing in the dust
insights.body: Twice Jesus stoops and writes on the ground (8:6, 8:8). What he wrote is never told, and guesses are only guesses. His words turn the trap: let the one without sin throw the first stone (8:7).

insights.title: Light of the world
insights.body: At the Feast of Tabernacles, great lamps were lit in the temple's Court of the Women and lit up the city. Jesus says, "I am the light of the world" (8:12), probably in the same court (8:20).

insights.title: The truth will make you free
insights.body: Jesus says the truth will make them free (8:32). His hearers say they have never been slaves (8:33), forgetting Egypt and Rome. Jesus means slavery to sin, from which only the Son sets people free (8:36).

insights.title: Children of Abraham
insights.body: The crowd claims Abraham as father; Jesus says Abraham's true children would do what Abraham did (8:39). Paul makes a similar argument: Abraham's children are those who share his faith.

insights.title: Before Abraham, I AM
insights.body: Jesus says, "Before Abraham came into existence, I AM" (8:58). He doesn't say "I was," but uses the absolute "I am," God's name from the burning bush. The crowd understands the claim and picks up stones (8:59).

insights.title: Neither do I condemn you
insights.body: Jesus tells the woman, "Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more" (8:11). Mercy and a call to change come together. (The passage is bracketed in many Bibles; see chapter 7.)

insights.title: The first stone
insights.body: Everyone walks away, oldest first (8:9). When are you quick to judge someone for a sin you share in another form?

9.summary: Jesus heals a man born blind; the Pharisees interrogate him and his parents, then throw him out, and the man comes to worship Jesus while the seeing leaders are called blind.
9.lookfor: Follow the healed man's growing understanding of Jesus, and notice who ends up blind at the end.

names.name: Siloam
names.gloss: A pool at the south end of Jerusalem fed by Hezekiah's tunnel.

insights.title: Who sinned?
insights.body: The disciples assume the man's blindness is punishment for sin, his or his parents' (9:2). Jesus rejects that: it is so the works of God may be revealed in him (9:3).

insights.title: Mud and the potter
insights.body: Jesus makes mud and puts it on the man's eyes (9:6). Some early Christian writers recalled God forming Adam from the dust: the Creator is making a new creation. It may also simply mirror a common healing practice.

insights.title: Siloam, Sent
insights.body: John translates Siloam as "Sent" (9:7). The man is sent to the pool named Sent, and John repeatedly calls Jesus the one sent by the Father.

insights.title: The pool found
insights.body: In 2004 workers in Jerusalem uncovered steps of a large pool from Jesus' time at the south end of the City of David, widely identified as the pool of Siloam.

insights.title: From a man to Lord
insights.body: Watch the man's titles for Jesus grow: "a man called Jesus" (9:11), "a prophet" (9:17), one from God (9:33), and finally "Lord, I believe" as he worships (9:38). His sight grows as the Pharisees' darkens.

insights.title: Put out of the synagogue
insights.body: The parents fear being put out of the synagogue (9:22). Many scholars think this reflects tensions late in the first century, when followers of Jesus were excluded from some synagogues; others place it in Jesus' own time.

insights.title: One thing I know
insights.body: The man can't win the theological debate, but he says, "One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see" (9:25). What has Jesus changed in you that you can simply tell?

10.summary: Jesus describes himself as the gate for the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down his life, and at the Feast of Dedication says, "I and the Father are one."
10.lookfor: Notice the difference between the shepherd and the hired hand, and why the crowd again picks up stones.

names.name: Solomon
names.gloss: Israel's king; a covered colonnade of the temple was named after him.

insights.title: The sheepfold
insights.body: Several flocks might share a walled fold at night, and each shepherd called his own sheep out by name (10:3). Sheep know their shepherd's voice and won't follow a stranger.

insights.title: The good shepherd
insights.body: "I am the good shepherd" (10:11) answers Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his people himself, through a son of David.

insights.title: Lays down his life
insights.body: The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (10:11), freely: no one takes it from him (10:18). The hired hand runs when the wolf comes because the sheep aren't his.

insights.title: Other sheep
insights.body: "I have other sheep, which are not of this fold" (10:16). Most readers take this as the Gentiles, who will join one flock under one shepherd.

insights.title: The Feast of Dedication
insights.body: The Feast of Dedication (10:22) is Hanukkah, celebrating the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after the Maccabees drove out the Seleucid king who had defiled it.

insights.title: I and the Father are one
insights.body: "I and the Father are one" (10:30). The word for one is neuter: one in nature or work, not one person. The crowd hears a claim to be God and reaches for stones (10:31-33).

insights.title: Called by name
insights.body: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name (10:3). How does it change your faith to know Jesus calls you by name?

11.summary: Jesus raises his friend Lazarus four days after death, telling Martha he is the resurrection and the life; the miracle leads the council to plot his death.
11.lookfor: Notice why Jesus waits two days, what he says to Martha, and the high priest's unintended prophecy.

names.name: Lazarus
names.gloss: Brother of Martha and Mary in Bethany, a close friend of Jesus.

names.name: Bethany
names.gloss: A village on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometers from Jerusalem.

names.name: Thomas
names.gloss: One of the twelve, also called Didymus, the Twin.

names.name: Caiaphas
names.gloss: The high priest that year.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: A town near the wilderness, north of Jerusalem.

insights.title: He stayed two days
insights.body: Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, so he stayed where he was two more days (11:5-6). John's "so" is startling: the delay is part of the love, leading to a greater sign.

insights.title: Four days
insights.body: By the time Jesus arrives Lazarus has been dead four days (11:17). A later Jewish belief held that the soul lingered near the body for three days; after four, death was beyond doubt.

insights.title: The resurrection and the life
insights.body: Martha believes in the resurrection at the last day; Jesus says, "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25). Resurrection isn't only a future event; it is a person standing in front of her.

insights.title: Jesus wept
insights.body: "Jesus wept" (11:35), the shortest verse in most English Bibles. He knows he is about to raise Lazarus, yet he weeps with those who weep. The word for his deep anger and distress (11:33) suggests outrage at death itself.

insights.title: The sign that leads to the cross
insights.body: Raising Lazarus is the last and greatest sign, and it triggers the plot to kill Jesus (11:53). Giving life to his friend costs Jesus his own.

insights.title: One man for the people
insights.body: Caiaphas argues it is better for one man to die than for the whole nation to perish (11:50). John says he unknowingly prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather God's scattered children into one (11:51-52).

insights.title: Do you believe this?
insights.body: Jesus asks Martha, "Do you believe this?" (11:26). If he is the resurrection, what changes about the losses you face?

12.summary: Mary anoints Jesus at Bethany, he rides into Jerusalem, Greeks ask to see him, and he speaks of his hour as a grain of wheat that must die; the chapter closes his public ministry.
12.lookfor: Notice who asks to see Jesus, and how he responds by talking about his hour and a seed dying.

names.name: Mary
names.gloss: Sister of Martha and Lazarus, who anoints Jesus.

names.name: Judas Iscariot
names.gloss: The disciple who kept the money bag and would betray Jesus.

names.name: Greeks
names.gloss: Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God and came up for the feast.

names.name: Isaiah
names.gloss: The eighth-century BC prophet whose words John quotes.

insights.title: A pound of nard
insights.body: Mary pours a pound of pure nard, a perfume from the Himalayas, on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair (12:3). It was worth three hundred denarii, about a year's wages (12:5). Jesus says she kept it for his burial (12:7).

insights.title: Palm branches
insights.body: The crowd waves palm branches (12:13), a symbol of Jewish national victory since the Maccabees, and shouts from Psalm 118. Jesus answers by riding a young donkey, Zechariah's humble king.

insights.title: The Greeks arrive
insights.body: Some Greeks ask Philip, "Sir, we want to see Jesus" (12:21). When Gentiles come seeking him, Jesus says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified (12:23): the whole world is now in view.

insights.title: A grain of wheat
insights.body: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it stays alone; if it dies, it bears much fruit (12:24). Jesus explains his death as a seed's death that produces a harvest.

insights.title: Lifted up, drawing all
insights.body: "I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself" (12:32). John explains this means the kind of death he would die: lifted on a cross.

insights.title: Isaiah saw his glory
insights.body: John quotes Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 on unbelief, then says Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory (12:41), Jesus' glory. The vision of the Lord on the throne is read as a vision of Christ.

insights.title: Loving praise
insights.body: Some leaders believed but kept quiet, loving people's praise more than God's (12:42-43). Where does fear of others' opinion silence your faith?

13.summary: At the last supper Jesus washes his disciples' feet, foretells his betrayal as Judas goes out into the night, gives the new commandment to love, and predicts Peter's denial.
13.lookfor: Notice what Jesus knows before he picks up the towel (13:3), and the words "it was night" when Judas leaves.

names.name: Simon Peter
names.gloss: Leader of the twelve, who resists having his feet washed.

insights.title: A slave's task
insights.body: Washing the feet of guests was a job for the lowest servant, and some Jewish teachers said even a Hebrew slave should not be made to do it. Jesus takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet (13:4-5).

insights.title: Knowing who he was
insights.body: John says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands and that he came from God and was going to God, so he washed their feet (13:3-5). Knowing his greatness frees him to serve.

insights.title: Unless I wash you
insights.body: Peter refuses, then asks for a full bath (13:8-9). Jesus says unless he washes him, Peter has no part with him: the washing pictures the cleansing only Jesus' death gives.

insights.title: And it was night
insights.body: Judas takes the bread and goes out immediately, "and it was night" (13:30). In John, night is more than the time; Judas walks out of the light into darkness.

insights.title: A new commandment
insights.body: Love was commanded in the law (13:34); what is new is the measure: as I have loved you. The church's distinguishing mark is love for one another (13:35).

insights.title: The beloved disciple
insights.body: One disciple, "whom Jesus loved," reclines next to him at the table (13:23). He is never named in John; tradition identifies him with John son of Zebedee, the source of this Gospel's witness.

insights.title: Washing feet today
insights.body: Jesus says, "You also ought to wash one another's feet" (13:14). What humble, unseen act of service is he asking of you?

14.summary: Jesus comforts his troubled disciples: he goes to prepare a place, he is the way, the truth and the life, the Father is seen in him, and he will send the Holy Spirit and leave them his peace.
14.lookfor: Notice the questions Thomas, Philip and Judas ask, and the name Jesus gives the Spirit.

names.name: Thomas
names.gloss: One of the twelve, who asks how they can know the way.

names.name: Philip
names.gloss: One of the twelve, who asks to be shown the Father.

names.name: Judas
names.gloss: Not Iscariot: another disciple of that name, probably Thaddaeus in other lists.

insights.title: Many rooms
insights.body: "In my Father's house are many homes" (14:2). Some see the picture of a family house where a groom added rooms for his bride; others recall the temple's many rooms. Either way, there is room for them with the Father.

insights.title: The way, the truth and the life
insights.body: Thomas asks how they can know the way; Jesus answers, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me" (14:6). The early church was simply called "the Way."

insights.title: Show us the Father
insights.body: Philip asks to see the Father; Jesus says whoever has seen him has seen the Father (14:9). Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown only his back; now God is seen in a face.

insights.title: Another Counselor
insights.body: Jesus promises another Counselor (14:16), the Greek paraklētos: one called alongside, a helper, advocate or comforter. "Another" means one like Jesus himself, who will be with them forever.

insights.title: Father, Son and Spirit
insights.body: In this chapter the Father sends, the Son asks, and the Spirit comes and teaches (14:16, 14:26). Passages like this shaped the church's later teaching on the Trinity, worked out at Nicaea and Constantinople.

insights.title: Peace I leave
insights.body: "Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives" (14:27). Shalom was the common greeting; Jesus gives it as a farewell gift, as his own peace.

insights.title: Let not your heart be troubled
insights.body: Jesus says this on the night of his betrayal, when he had every reason to be troubled himself (14:1). What troubles your heart that you need to hand to him?

15.summary: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his disciples the branches, calls them friends, commands them to love one another, and warns that the world will hate them as it hated him.
15.lookfor: Count how often Jesus says "remain," and notice what he now calls his disciples instead of servants.

insights.title: The true vine
insights.body: Israel was often pictured as God's vine or vineyard, frequently one that failed to bear fruit. "I am the true vine" (15:1): Jesus is the faithful Israel, and his followers bear fruit by being joined to him.

insights.title: Remain
insights.body: The Greek menō, remain or abide, appears about ten times in 15:4-10. Fruit doesn't come from effort alone but from staying connected: apart from me you can do nothing (15:5).

insights.title: Pruning
insights.body: Vinedressers cut away dead wood and also prune fruitful branches so they bear more (15:2). The pruning of fruitful branches is painful but purposeful.

insights.title: No longer servants but friends
insights.body: Jesus calls his disciples friends, because he has told them everything he heard from the Father (15:15). Abraham was called God's friend; now all disciples are.

insights.title: Greater love
insights.body: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (15:13). Jesus says this hours before doing it.

insights.title: Hated without a cause
insights.body: The world will hate the disciples as it hated Jesus (15:18). He quotes a psalm, "They hated me without a cause" (15:25), applying David's lament to himself.

insights.title: Fruit that remains
insights.body: Jesus chose them to bear fruit that remains (15:16). What in your life now will still matter in fifty years?

16.summary: Jesus warns of coming persecution, explains that the Spirit will convict the world and guide them into truth, and promises that their grief will turn to joy like a mother after birth.
16.lookfor: Notice why Jesus says it is good for them that he leaves, and the picture of the woman in labor.

insights.title: Better that I go
insights.body: Jesus says it is to their advantage that he goes away, because then the Counselor will come (16:7). The Spirit's presence everywhere is better than Jesus' bodily presence in one place.

insights.title: Sin, righteousness, judgment
insights.body: The Spirit will convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgment (16:8-11): sin in not believing, righteousness shown by Jesus going to the Father, judgment because the ruler of this world is already condemned.

insights.title: Into all truth
insights.body: The Spirit will guide them into all the truth (16:13), not speaking on his own but taking what is Jesus' and declaring it. The apostles' teaching, later written, is seen as the fruit of this promise.

insights.title: A woman in labor
insights.body: Jesus compares their coming grief to a woman in labor, whose pain gives way to joy at the birth (16:21). The prophets used labor pains for the trouble before God's new age.

insights.title: In my name
insights.body: Jesus says the Father will give whatever they ask in his name (16:23-24). To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as his representative, for what he would want, not to add a magic formula.

insights.title: I have overcome the world
insights.body: The farewell discourse ends: in the world you have trouble, but cheer up, I have overcome the world (16:33). He says this before the cross, as if it had already happened.

insights.title: Joy no one can take
insights.body: Jesus promises a joy no one will take away (16:22). How is that different from the happiness circumstances give and take?

17.summary: Jesus prays to the Father: for his own glorification, for his disciples to be kept and made holy in the truth, and for all who will believe through them to be one.
17.lookfor: Notice the three groups Jesus prays for, and what he says eternal life is (17:3).

insights.title: The high-priestly prayer
insights.body: Since the sixteenth century this chapter has been called Jesus' high-priestly prayer: like the high priest, he intercedes for his people before offering himself. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded.

insights.title: What eternal life is
insights.body: Jesus defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (17:3). It is a relationship that begins now, not only endless time later.

insights.title: Sanctify them
insights.body: "Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth" (17:17). To sanctify is to set apart for God; Jesus sets himself apart (17:19) so that they may be set apart too.

insights.title: In the world, not of it
insights.body: Jesus doesn't pray for his followers to be taken out of the world but to be kept from the evil one (17:15). They are sent into the world as he was sent (17:18).

insights.title: That they may be one
insights.body: Jesus prays for all who will believe through the apostles' word, that they may be one as the Father and Son are one, so that the world may believe (17:20-21). This prayer has shaped Christian efforts at unity across traditions.

insights.title: The glory before the world
insights.body: Jesus asks to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (17:5), returning to the opening of the Gospel: the Word with God in the beginning.

insights.title: Prayed for
insights.body: Jesus prayed for those who would believe through the disciples' message (17:20), and that includes you. How does it feel to know you were in his prayer that night?

18.summary: Jesus is arrested in a garden, questioned by Annas while Peter denies him three times, and brought to Pilate, who asks whether he is a king and what truth is.
18.lookfor: Notice what happens when Jesus says "I am he" to the soldiers, and Pilate's question about truth.

names.name: Kidron
names.gloss: A valley east of Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives.

names.name: Malchus
names.gloss: The high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off.

names.name: Annas
names.gloss: A former high priest, father-in-law of Caiaphas, still powerful.

names.name: Caiaphas
names.gloss: The serving high priest.

names.name: Pilate
names.gloss: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea.

names.name: Barabbas
names.gloss: A prisoner John calls a robber, released instead of Jesus.

insights.title: They fell to the ground
insights.body: When Jesus says "I am he" to the arresting party, they draw back and fall to the ground (18:6). The same words, egō eimi, carry divine weight. Jesus isn't captured; he gives himself up.

insights.title: A garden
insights.body: John alone calls the place of arrest a garden (18:1), and Jesus is buried in a garden too (19:41). Some readers see an echo of Eden: what was lost in a garden is won back in one.

insights.title: A charcoal fire
insights.body: Peter warms himself at a charcoal fire as he denies Jesus (18:18). The only other charcoal fire in the New Testament is by the lake in chapter 21, where the risen Jesus restores him.

insights.title: Not entering the governor's house
insights.body: The leaders won't enter Pilate's headquarters so they won't be defiled before eating the Passover (18:28). John notes the irony: careful about ritual purity while seeking an innocent man's death.

insights.title: My kingdom is not of this world
insights.body: Jesus tells Pilate, "My Kingdom is not of this world" (18:36). He doesn't mean it is unreal or only spiritual, but that it doesn't come from or work by this world's power; otherwise his servants would fight.

insights.title: What is truth?
insights.body: Jesus says he came to testify to the truth; Pilate replies, "What is truth?" (18:38) and walks out without an answer. The reader knows the answer is standing before him.

insights.title: Standing by the fire
insights.body: Peter stays near Jesus but blends in with the crowd at the fire. Where are you tempted to stay close to Jesus without being known as his?

19.summary: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked, then hands him over to be crucified; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, says "It is finished," and is buried by Joseph and Nicodemus.
19.lookfor: Notice the sign over the cross in three languages, and the words Jesus speaks before he dies.

names.name: Gabbatha
names.gloss: Aramaic name for the stone pavement where Pilate judged.

names.name: Golgotha
names.gloss: Aramaic for Place of a Skull, outside the city walls.

names.name: Clopas
names.gloss: Husband of one of the Marys at the cross.

names.name: Magdalene
names.gloss: Mary Magdalene, a follower of Jesus and first witness of the resurrection.

names.name: Arimathaea
names.gloss: Hometown of Joseph, a secret disciple who buried Jesus.

names.name: Nicodemus
names.gloss: The Pharisee who first came by night, now openly helping with the burial.

insights.title: The sixth hour
insights.body: John says it was about the sixth hour, noon, on the day of preparation for the Passover when Pilate handed Jesus over (19:14), the time when Passover lambs began to be slaughtered in the temple. Mark gives a different hour, and scholars discuss how the two timings relate.

insights.title: We have no king but Caesar
insights.body: The chief priests say, "We have no king but Caesar!" (19:15). Leaders of the nation that confessed God as its king now confess Rome's emperor.

insights.title: In three languages
insights.body: Pilate's sign, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, was written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (19:20): the languages of worship, empire and culture. The whole world is told who he is.

insights.title: Lots for his clothing
insights.body: The soldiers cast lots for Jesus' seamless tunic (19:23-24), fulfilling Psalm 22, the psalm that begins "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"

insights.title: It is finished
insights.body: Jesus' last word is a single Greek word, tetelestai (19:30): it is finished, completed, accomplished. The work the Father gave him is done.

insights.title: Not a bone broken
insights.body: The soldiers don't break Jesus' legs (19:33), and John sees fulfilled the rule that no bone of the Passover lamb be broken. Blood and water flow from his pierced side, fulfilling Zechariah: they will look on him whom they pierced (19:36-37).

insights.title: Secret disciples
insights.body: Joseph had been a secret disciple out of fear, and Nicodemus came by night; at the cross both come into the open (19:38-39). What would make you step out of the shadows?

20.summary: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty; Peter and the beloved disciple see the grave clothes; the risen Jesus meets Mary in the garden, appears to the disciples, and then to doubting Thomas.
20.lookfor: Notice when Mary recognizes Jesus, and Thomas's confession, the climax of the Gospel.

names.name: Mary Magdalene
names.gloss: The first person to see the risen Jesus.

names.name: Didymus
names.gloss: Greek for the Twin, Thomas's other name.

insights.title: The grave clothes
insights.body: The linen cloths lie there, and the face cloth is rolled up in a place by itself (20:6-7). Grave robbers would hardly unwrap a body and leave the cloths neatly. The beloved disciple sees and believes (20:8).

insights.title: She thought he was the gardener
insights.body: Mary mistakes Jesus for the gardener (20:15) and recognizes him only when he says her name (20:16), just as the good shepherd calls his sheep by name.

insights.title: Apostle to the apostles
insights.body: Jesus sends Mary to tell the disciples (20:17), and she goes and tells them that she has seen the Lord (20:18). Early church writers called her the apostle to the apostles.

insights.title: He breathed on them
insights.body: Jesus breathes on the disciples and says, "Receive the Holy Spirit!" (20:22). The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament when God breathes life into Adam: a new creation begins.

insights.title: My Lord and my God
insights.body: Thomas, who demanded proof, makes the fullest confession in the Gospels: "My Lord and my God!" (20:28). The Gospel that opened with the Word who was God ends its main story with a disciple saying so to Jesus' face.

insights.title: Why this book was written
insights.body: John says Jesus did many other signs, but these are written so that readers may believe and have life in his name (20:30-31). The purpose of the whole Gospel is stated here.

insights.title: Blessed are those who haven't seen
insights.body: Jesus says to Thomas, "Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed" (20:29). That includes every reader since. What helps you believe without seeing?

21.summary: By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus gives the disciples a great catch, eats breakfast with them, restores Peter with three questions of love, and speaks of Peter's death and the beloved disciple.
21.lookfor: Count Jesus' three questions to Peter and compare them with Peter's three denials.

names.name: Tiberias
names.gloss: Another name for the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Nathanael
names.gloss: A disciple from Cana in Galilee.

names.name: Zebedee
names.gloss: Father of the disciples James and John.

insights.title: One hundred fifty-three
insights.body: The net holds 153 large fish and doesn't tear (21:11). Readers since Jerome have suggested symbolic meanings, such as all the kinds of fish then known, picturing a mission to all nations; it may simply be an eyewitness's count.

insights.title: Breakfast on a charcoal fire
insights.body: Jesus has a charcoal fire burning with fish and bread (21:9). The last charcoal fire was where Peter denied him (18:18). The scene of failure becomes the scene of restoration.

insights.title: Do you love me?
insights.body: Jesus asks Peter three times if he loves him (21:15-17). The Greek alternates two verbs for love, agapaō and phileō; some see a significant difference, while many scholars think John is simply varying his words. The threefold question matches the threefold denial.

insights.title: Feed my sheep
insights.body: Jesus answers each of Peter's replies with a task: feed my lambs, shepherd my sheep (21:15-17). The good shepherd entrusts his flock to the one who failed him. Peter later urges church leaders to shepherd God's flock.

insights.title: Stretch out your hands
insights.body: Jesus says that when Peter is old, others will stretch out his hands and lead him where he doesn't want to go (21:18-19), indicating the death by which he would glorify God. Early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero.

insights.title: The beloved disciple's witness
insights.body: The Gospel ends by naming the beloved disciple as the one who testifies and wrote these things, and adds "we know that his witness is true" (21:24). The world itself could not contain all the books if everything were written (21:25).

insights.title: What is that to you?
insights.body: When Peter asks about the other disciple's future, Jesus says, "What is that to you? You follow me" (21:22). Where do you compare your path with someone else's instead of following?

intro.who: Church tradition from Irenaeus in the second century names John, son of Zebedee, the disciple whom Jesus loved (21:20-24). Many modern scholars see that beloved disciple as the source of the witness, with his followers shaping the final text.
intro.when: Most scholars date it to about AD 90–100, making it the last of the four Gospels; a minority argue for an earlier date. It covers Jesus' ministry over about three Passovers.
intro.why: John says he chose these signs so that readers would believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:31).
